Judgment
Amal Ranaraja. J,
1. The accused-appellant (hereinafter referred to as the ‘appellant’) has
been indicted in the High Court of Colombo in case no. HC 3849/22.
The charges in the indictment are as follows;
01. On or around the 11th of October, 2012, within the jurisdiction
of this Court, in Aduruppu Weediya, Colombo, you have
committed rape against one Fathima Munasa Mubharak, a minor
under the age of 16; thereby you have committed an offence
punishable under Section 364 (2) read with Section 364(2)(e) of
the Penal Code of Sri Lanka as amended by the Penal Code
(Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995.
02. On a date between the 12th of October, 2012 and 11th of
February, 2013, within the jurisdiction of this Court, in
Aduruppu Weediya, Colombo, you have committed rape against
one Fathima Munasa Mubharak, a minor under the age of 16;
thereby you have committed an offence punishable under
Section 364 (2) read with Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code of
Sri Lanka as amended by the Penal Code (Amendment) Act No.
03. At the same time and location as the above second charge, but,
at a separate occasion than that of the above second charge, you
have committed rape against one Fathima Munasa Mubharak, a
minor under the age of 16; thereby you have committed an
offence punishable under Section 364 (2) read with Section
364(2)(e) of the Penal Code of Sri Lanka as amended by the Penal
Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995.
2. At the conclusion of the trial, the learned High Court Judge has
convicted the appellant of the charges and sentenced him as follows;
i. 15 years rigorous imprisonment each, in respect of the first,
second and third charges. Also, has imposed a fine of
Rs.10,000.00, with a term of 6 months rigorous imprisonment
each in default, in respect of the first, second, and third charges.
Further, the appellant has also been directed to pay a sum of
Rs.250,000.00 to PW01 as compensation with a term of 2 years
rigorous imprisonment in default.
It has been directed that the substantive terms of rigorous
imprisonment shall run concurrently.
3. The appellant, being aggrieved by the conviction, disputed judgement
together with the sentencing order has preferred the instant appeal to
this Court
Case of the Prosecution
4. PW01 has been born on March 15th, 1997. Her father has passed away
when she was 11 years old and she has lived in a house in the Aduruppu
Weediya area with her mother and sister at the time in issue.
5. Following an incident of cheating, PW01 and her mother have lodged a
complaint at the Mount Lavinia Police Station. The appellant, a police
officer attached to the station at that time, has recorded the complaint.
During this interaction, an acquaintance has developed between PW01
and the appellant, which has later evolved into a romantic relationship.
The appellant has visited PW01’s residence on several occasions and
engaged in sexual intercourse with her at times.
6. However, when the appellant’s family had objected to a marriage with
PW01, the appellant has allegedly distanced himself from her. Despite
PW01’s attempts to contact the appellant, she has been unsuccessful.
As a result, PW01 has lodged a complaint against the appellant and an
investigation commenced.
7. Dr. K.S. Dahanayake, MD (Forensic Medicine), has examined PW01. The
medico-legal report has been produced as evidence and marked පැ01.
The register of births bearing number 5009, and relevant to PW01’s
birth registration, has also been produced as evidence and marked
Case of the Appellant
8. Although the appellant has admitted to being in a romantic relationship
with PW01, he has denied engaging in sexual intercourse with her.
Grounds of appeal
9. When the matter was taken up for argument the learned counsel
appearing on behalf of the appellant raised the following grounds of
appeal;
I. The learned Trial Judge has failed to evaluate the case for the
prosecution and the evidence of the case adequately.
II. The contradictions of the witness for the prosecution and the
contradictions between the two prosecution witnesses have not
been considered adequately, causing much prejudice to the
accused Appellant.
III. The subsequent conduct of the prosecutrix has been
unreasonably held against the accused.
IV. The learned Trial Judge has misdirected himself on the
medical evidence.
V. The strong evidence of motive for false implication has been
totally disregarded, causing much prejudice to the accused-
appellant.
VI. Due consideration has not been given to the dock statement
of the accused, which is valid evidence.
VII. Due to one or more of the above reasons, the accused
appellant has been denied a fair trial, a constitutionally
guaranteed right to every person charged with a criminal
offence.
10. PW01 has testified as follows;

It is stated that, beginning December 2012, the appellant has visited
PW01 at her residence situated in Aduruppu Weediya area and engaged
in sexual intercourse with her on multiple occasions. PW01 has further
stated that approximately ten such encounters have occurred within
one and half months. Further, born on March 15th, 1997, PW01 has
been a 15 year old girl at that time.
11. Following a complaint lodged against the appellant, an investigation
has commenced. During this investigation, PW01 has been presented
to Dr. K.S. Dahanayake, MD (Forensic Medicine), for an examination.
Prior to conducting the examination, Dr. Dahanayake has recorded the
patient’s history. PW01 has then made the following statement;
Vide Page 355 of the Brief
12. It is stated that when PW01 was eleven years old, a person identified as
Ghouse engaged in sexual intercourse with PW01 under threat.
Subsequently, PW01 reportedly began a romantic relationship with the
appellant. It is further stated that PW01 and the appellant engaged in
consensual sexual intercourse on approximately eleven occasions. It
being so, PW01 has been consistent and trustworthy as regards to her
narrative involving the appellant.
13. First and foremost, consistency in a prosecutrix’s statement serves as
a fundamental indicator of truthfulness. In cases of sexual abuse, it is
not uncommon for victims to initially confront the trauma through
varied accounts as they grapple with the emotional and psychological
implications of the experience.
14. However, when a prosecutrix’s account remains consistent across
different instances, whether in police statements, Court testimonies or
other settings, such consistency reinforces the validity of her claims.
Courts must recognise that, in situations laden with psychological
complexity, mere existence of a consistent narrative can be a powerful
testament in the absence of additional corroborative evidence.
15. Moreover, trustworthiness is a critical factor that influences the
evaluation of a prosecutrix’s testimony. A trustworthy prosecutrix is
forthcoming about her experiences and maintains a clear recollection
of events. This factor becomes particularly relevant in sexual abuse
cases, where societal scepticism can often cloud judgement regarding
victims. The governing principle should be that, in assessing credibility
of a prosecutrix, the Court should prioritise her assertiveness,
coherence, and the emotional sincerity with which she expresses her
ordeal.
16. In the case of Premasiri vs. Attorney General [2006] 3 Sri. LR 106, Eric
Basnayake J, has held,
“There is no rule that there must be corroboration in every case, before
a conviction can be allowed to stand. It is well settled law that a
conviction for the offence of rape can be based on the sole testimony of
the prosecutrix, if it is reliable, unimpeachable and there is no
in<irmity;”
17. Further, in the case of Sunil and Another vs. Attorney General [1986] 1
Sri. LR 230, Dheeraratne J, has held,
“I think it is perfectly legitimate for a judge, in a case of this nature,
to direct a jury that if they <ind the evidence of the complainant
so convincing, they could act on that evidence alone, even in the
absence of her evidence being corroborated.”
18. Regarding the medico-legal report Dr. Dahanyake, has described the
nature, size, shape, disposition and the sight of injuries as follows;

19. He has then provided his opinion on whether the injuries are consistent
with the history of the patient stating as follows;
Vide Page 12 of the Brief
20. This opinion corroborates PW01’s testimony regarding her multiple
incidents of sexual intercourse with a person named Ghouse and with
the appellant. Furthermore, it reinforces the conclusion that PW01 was
a truthful witness. PW01 has also categorically rejected the suggestions
presented to her, namely that the appellant had not engaged in sexual
intercourse with her and that he had been falsely implicated by PW01.
21. The appellant in his dock statement has asserted that he did not engage
in sexual intercourse with PW01. He has further claimed that PW01 has
had a romantic relationship with another police officer, whose name
has been mentioned, and that PW01 has previously been a victim of
gang rape while working at a club. These assertions have been aimed
to distance him from any incriminating evidence of sexual intercourse
with PW01.
22. However, despite the appellant suggesting these instances of third party
involvement, these specific allegations have not been put to PW01
during her cross examination. These omissions suggest that these
claims had been an afterthought on the appellant’s part, rather than
points raised at the earliest opportunity. The learned High Court Judge
has considered these material omissions before deciding not to act on
the appellant’s statement.
23. In the case of Pilippu Mandige Nalaka Krishantha Kumara Thisera v A.G
(CA87/2005) decided on 17.05.2007, Sisira de Abrew J, has held
“...I hold that whenever evidence given by a witness on a material point
is not challenged in cross examination, it has to be concluded that such
evidence is not disputed and is accepted by the opponent subject of
course to the quali<ication that the witness is a reliable witness.”
24. Further, in the case of Sivathasan vs. Attorney General [2021] 2 SLR
290, Kodagoda, J, has stated,
“It would therefore be seen that suggestions to prosecution witnesses
are very important, and inter-alia serve as an opportunity for the
defence to place before prosecution witnesses the position of the
defence. It enables the Court to take early cognizance of the position of
the defence and also enable prosecution witnesses to respond to the
defence position. That the defence placed before Court their position at
the <irst available opportunity also enables it to satisfy the ‘test of
spontaneity’. Therefore, it is of importance that the defence uses this
opportunity to speci<ically and in unambiguous terms indicate both to
the Court and to prosecution witnesses, the position of the defence.
Should the defence not make use of this opportunity and take up a
particular position for the <irst time during the case for the defence,
that position will suffer from the weakness of ‘belatedness’.”
25. In those circumstances I am not inclined to interfere with the
conviction, disputed judgement together with the sentencing order and
proceed to affirm the same. The substantive terms of rigorous
imprisonment shall run concurrently and begin from the date of
conviction, i.e. September 3rd, 2024.
26. I dismiss the appeal but make no order regarding costs.
Appeal dismissed.
27. The Registrar of this Court is directed to send this Judgement to the
